page_title: What does retrieval add? Re-evaluating DBLP-QA
lede: Dewey answers questions about dblp by retrieving before it answers. This study asks how much retrieval actually helps on DBLP-QA, a scholarly QA benchmark built by dblp's own team - graded automatically, repeatably, and by two judges from different model families.

findings.title: Answering is solved; finding is not
findings.text: Given the abstract a question was written from, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini and Mistral-7B all score at least 1.96 of 2, on both question sets. What still separates systems is whether retrieval finds that abstract.

findings.title: Models know the field, not the papers
findings.text: Without retrieval gpt-4.1 scores 1.46 on DBLP-QA, where 58% of questions are general knowledge. On 100 new questions about 2025-2026 papers it scores 1.04 - but on paper-specific questions it scores the same on old and new papers (1.00 vs 1.02), so the models were not remembering DBLP-QA's papers.

findings.title: In the open world, BM25 is enough
findings.text: The original index cannot be rebuilt, so retrieval was reconstructed from four public search services. The right paper reaches the top five for 58% of DBLP-QA questions and 89% of the new ones; BM25 gets within two points of the candidates' ceiling, and hybrid retrieval adds nothing.

findings.title: The gain follows retrieval success
findings.text: The share of the right abstract's gain that RAG recovers tracks how often retrieval finds it: about 56% at 58% retrieval, about 82% at 89%, for every model.

findings.title: Wrong papers do not hurt - single-reference grading does
findings.text: Graded against the one reference answer, wrong papers seem to cost up to 0.4 points. Graded so that any correct answer counts, after controls, neither judge finds a measurable cost: the models give different correct answers, not wrong ones.

findings.title: Selective retrieval saves time, not accuracy
findings.text: A prompt that allows ignoring irrelevant abstracts helps only gpt-4.1, slightly. A relevance gate does not improve accuracy, but a 7B model reading 1.7 abstracts instead of 5 answers twice as fast at the same score.

results.caption: Mean score (0-2) graded by gpt-4.1. RAG: BM25 over a frozen candidate pool, top five abstracts. Oracle: the abstract the question was written from.

recovery.caption: The share of the right abstract's gain over no retrieval that plain RAG recovers, against how often the right paper reaches the context (gpt-4.1 judge). The dashed line is where the two are equal.

dewey: Dewey answers questions about dblp's records - people, venues, counts, co-authors - by calling tools over the full dump, so its answers come from data, not from memory. Questions about what a paper says are the harder case this study measures.

Dewey's paper search is the study's dblp-search: a hybrid search over every dblp title. On its own it finds the right paper within its top 50 for 32% of DBLP-QA questions and 73% of the fresh ones; adding abstract search (OpenAlex) and BM25 re-ranking over abstracts lifts the top five to 58% and 89%.
The study's evaluation harness lives in the same codebase as Dewey and runs on the same machine, so the next version of Dewey can be measured the same way.
